How viruses were discovered
Virology evolved later than bacteriology
• The comparatively large size of bacteria made them visible 
even with the simple microscope
• However, although the physical nature of 
viruses was not fully revealed until the 
invention of the electron microscope the 
infections they caused have been known and 
feared since the dawn of history

Mummy of Rameses V. The lesions of 
the face are suggestive of smallpox
Scientists 
are 
discovering 
and 
resurrecting ancient viruses trapped in 
permafrost and frozen remains.

• The Latin word for virus  means ‘poisonous fluid 
• In Pasteur’s  laboratory, Charles Chamberlnd devised 
a filtre that would hold back even the smallest 
bacteria.
•  Iwanowski in Russia and Beijerink in Holland both 
showed that a plant infection, tobacco mosaic, could 
be transmitted by extracts that had been passed 
through a chamberland  filtre and hence could not 
contain bacteria.

• Foot-and-mouth disease of cattle was 
also transmitted by bacteria free filtrates 
, therefore,
• Living agents smaller than any known 
bacteria but capable of multiplying could 
cause a wide range of disease in plants 
and animals
•  New viruses are still being discovered 
often 
with 
new 
human 
infections 
originating from viruses in wild animals 
and birds in remote spot of the planet
• MERS CoV is an example emerging in 
2013 from camels in Saudi Arabia 
• The hemorrhagic fever Ebola re emerged 
most likely from bats in West Africa in 
2014
• SARS CoV-2 came from a thumb-sized 
bat tucked inside a remote Chinese cave 
2019
•In the 1930s, a new technology made viruses visible by microscopy

How they were grown in the laboratory
• Scientists realised that whatever it was that caused tobacco mosaic would grow 
only in living cells and could not be cultivated in the media used for bacteria.
• At that time there was no way of growing cells in the laboratory and so that all 
the early work on virus infections had to be done with intact plants or animals.
• Pasture used dogs and rabbits in the development of a rabies vaccine
• smallpox vaccine was cultivated on the shaved skin of calves and sheep
• in 1938 a virus was first grown in the laboratory in suspensions of minced 
kidney tissues. The two scientists who developed the knew cell culture later 
grew polio for the first time and were worthy recipients of the Nobel Prize

• During the following decades a great advance was made with the propagation of 
many viruses in developing chick embryos including yellow fever, smallpox and 
influenza
• The really big breakthrough came with the discovery of antibiotics in the 1940s a 
1950s until then it was very difficult to keep cell and tissue culture free from 
contamination with airborne bacteria and moulds
• Now, we have the ability to identify, isolate clone and express specific nucleotide 
sequences 
• This has led to the identification of history to unknown viruses that is still cannot 
be propagated in the laboratory laboratory by conventional methods such as 
hepatitis C 
• Micro -arrays which are in essence glass microscope slides containing hundreds 
of thousands of short or legal neglected 's that can capture a spectrum of virus 
genomes to survey samples where the identity of the virus is unknown 
• Next generation sequencing

Viruses are different from living cells, yet they make a large 
impact on cells
• They are “acellular” (not cells).
• They have no metabolism and cannot grow.
• They depend on host cells to make copies of themselves.
• They are the ultimate parasite; cannot replicate unless they are in host cell using that 
cell’s machinery
• Their origin is uncertain.
• They seem to have collected pieces of nucleic acid from various sources.
• They can infect nearly all lifeforms.
• They are not only species specific but tissue specific (as far as what they will infect)

Virus size and imaging
• Almost all viruses are too small to be seen with light microscopes.
• A single virus particle (a “virion”) may be only 20 nm across.
• Electron microscopes can magnify 500,000x.
• The image clarity is due to good resolution (0.05 nm).
• The invention of electron microscopes led to the discovery of many types of 
viruses in many types of organisms.
Size comparison: virions are much smaller than the bacterial and eukaryotic cells shown.

Virus evolution
• Did they “devolve” from free-living cells?
• Did nucleic acid molecules “escape” from 
cells?
• Did they begin as self-replicating molecules?

Virus morphology
• Each virion has:
• Nucleic acid: might be DNA or 
RNA, 
double 
stranded 
or 
single stranded
• Protein capsid
• Some 
virions 
also 
have 
an 
“envelope” that is similar to a 
cell membrane.

Four virus 
shapes

Bacteriophage 
T4

bacteria
• Infects the bacterium, 
Escherichia coli
• Has a DNA genome
• Has been studied 
extensively

Adenovirus
• Infects the human 
respiratory tract
• Is non-enveloped
• Other non-enveloped 
viruses include poliovirus, 
human papillomavirus, 
and hepatitis A virus.

HIV Retrovirus
• Causes AIDS (acquired 
immunodeficiency 
syndrome)
• Is enveloped
• Is a retrovirus (can reverse 
transcribe its RNA genome 
into DNA form.)

Viruses have genomes
• The virus core contains nucleic acid
• either DNA or RNA (but not both)
• may be single-stranded or double-stranded
• may be circular or linear
• may be in one piece or in multiple segments
• The genome is much smaller than a cell’s genome
• DNA directs the host cell to make new virus copies
• RNA may be directly transcribed, or replicated first.
• RNA viruses use enzymes that make more errors
• RNA viruses mutate more frequently

Several ways to classify viruses
• According to nucleic acid type and function
• According to capsid structure
• Enveloped/non-enveloped
• Genome structure

Cytopathic effects
• These cell damaging changes can occur when a virus replicates in a host cell:
• lysis (the cell ruptures or bursts open)*
• apoptosis (programmed self-destruction)
• widespread symptoms due to the body’s immune response
• *In some cases, replicated viruses can leave the cell by “budding”, which does not 
immediately kill the cell.

Steps of virus infections
• Attachment
• Entry
• Replication and Assembly
• Egress (Release)

Attachment
• Receptors on the surface of the host cell bind to virus capsid proteins or virus 
envelope glycoproteins
• Viruses can attach only to cells that have the right receptor molecules
• Therefore, viruses can be very specific about what species or cell type they can 
infect.

Entry
• Bacteriophage DNA enters the host cell “naked”.
• Viruses may enter eukaryotic cells by endocytosis or, 
if enveloped, by fusion with the cell’s membrane.

HIV, an enveloped, icosahedral virus, attaches to the CD4 receptor of an immune cell and 
fuses with the cell membrane. Viral contents are released into the cell, where viral enzymes 
convert the single-strandd RNA genome into DNA and incorporate it into the host genome.

Prions: 
proteinaceous infectious particles
• Very small
• Contain no nucleic acid
• Cause fatal neurodegenerative diseases
• Mad cow disease (BSE, bovine spongiform encephalopathy)
• Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (in humans)
• Kuru (in humans, spread by cannibalism) 
• Scrapie (in sheep)
• Chronic wasting disease (in deer, moose, elk)
• Prions are not destroyed by cooking

Viroids: 
small circles of RNA
• Only known to infect plants
• Can replicate within cells
• Do not manufacture any proteins
• Can cause crop failures

editorialNotes: Source slides are preserved unchanged. Cards clarify misleading source statements rather than repeating them as facts.
Slide 5 does not establish the exact animal, cave or route responsible for SARS-CoV-2 emergence. The precise emergence pathway remains unresolved; no exact-origin claim is memorised.
Historical culture statements on slides 7–8 are treated as historical context. Hepatitis C can now be propagated in specialised cell-culture systems.
Envelope status is separate from capsid shape. Mature HIV has a conical capsid core, despite slide 41 describing it as icosahedral.

Varicella-zoster latency usually involves episomal DNA in sensory neurons, not obligatory integration into the host chromosome. HPV integration can occur in cancer progression but is not required for every infection.
Positive-sense RNA can function as mRNA; negative-sense and double-stranded RNA viruses need RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to produce mRNA. Retroviruses instead use a DNA intermediate.
Baltimore slide 22 shows groups II–VI. Groups I and VII are added as explicitly identified completion of the standard seven-group framework.
RNA viruses often mutate rapidly, but proofreading and replication mechanisms differ; this is not a universal claim about every RNA virus.
Visual identification cards use figure crops with answer headings excluded. Supporting labelled panels appear after reveal. Original sources remain available in Slide reference.
Embedded video-placeholder slides 23–24 and 40 are preserved as references; unavailable video contents are not invented.
